passage:
It was show-and-tell day at the kindergarten. Parveen held up a small box of sheer khurma. "On Eid, my Nani makes this. We wake up early, wear new clothes and go to everyone's house."
"Do all families do that?" asked a classmate.
Parveen thought. "This is how my family does it."
Vikas, the teacher, smiled. "Thank you, Parveen. Who else has a family festival?" Hands flew up.

qa.q: What did Parveen hold up at show-and-tell?
qa.a: She held up a small box of sheer khurma.

qa.q: How might Parveen have felt when the classmate asked if all families do that?
qa.a: She may have felt a little unsure at first, so she paused before answering that this is how her family does it.

qa.q: How did Vikas help the class learn from Parveen's share?
qa.a: He thanked her and invited others to share their family festivals.

qa.q: How might classmates feel after Parveen's story?
qa.a: They might feel curious and eager to share their own traditions.

grounding: It shows a child sharing a festival tradition and understanding it as her family's way.

passage: I'm Payal, and my cousin Hrithik is five. On Onam morning he helped Ammamma lay flowers for the pookalam in the courtyard. He carefully put yellow petals in the middle. "This is how we do it," he told me, very serious, "the yellow goes first." I'm not sure where he got that rule, but Ammamma nodded. Later, he sat still on the floor for the sadya and ate the payasam last, like the grown-ups.

qa.q: What colour petals did Hrithik put in the middle?
qa.a: He put yellow petals in the middle.

qa.q: What does Hrithik's serious "This is how we do it" suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he feels proud and sure of his family's way of making the pookalam.

qa.q: How could Ammamma help Hrithik learn more about Onam?
qa.a: She could tell him a folk story about the festival while they make the pookalam.

qa.q: How does Payal see Hrithik's rule?
qa.a: Payal isn't sure where he got it, but notices Ammamma agrees with him.

grounding: An older cousin observes a child taking part in a festival tradition as his family's way.

passage:
Friday: Devika helped Vidya shape small clay diyas for Diwali. Her fingers got muddy.
Saturday: Vidya told her the story of Rama coming home and the people lighting lamps. Devika asked, "Did they have diyas like ours?"
Sunday night: The family lit rows of lamps. Devika held the first one. "In our house, the first diya is for Nana," she said. Vidya's eyes were wet.

qa.q: What did Devika help Vidya shape on Friday?
qa.a: She helped her shape small clay diyas.

qa.q: Why might Vidya's eyes be wet when Devika spoke?
qa.a: She was likely moved that Devika remembered the family custom of the first diya for Nana.

qa.q: How did Vidya help Devika understand the tradition?
qa.a: She included her in making diyas and told her the story behind the lamps.

qa.q: How might Devika's words affect the rest of the family?
qa.a: They may feel touched and proud that the youngest carries on the family tradition. 🪔

grounding: It shows a child taking part in festival preparations and understanding her family's way.

passage:
It poured all Diwali evening, and the courtyard where Parul's family always made rangoli was a puddle. Parul, five, pressed her nose to the window.

"No rangoli this year?" she wailed.

Her big brother Ujjwal thought, then spread newspaper on the living room floor. "Our family always makes one. We'll just make it inside."

They used rice flour and turmeric. Parul pressed her small handprint in the middle, like Ma did every year.

"This is our Diwali way," she said, very proud.

qa.q: What did they use to make the rangoli indoors?
qa.a: They used rice flour and turmeric.

qa.q: What was Parul feeling when she saw the courtyard?
qa.a: She was upset and disappointed, pressing her nose to the window and wailing that there would be no rangoli.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal do that helped keep the tradition?
qa.a: He adapted the tradition by moving it indoors, showing that the family's way could continue despite the rain.

qa.q: How might Ma feel seeing Parul's handprint in the rangoli?
qa.a: She would probably feel touched that Parul copied her own yearly habit.

grounding: Shows a young child keeping a family festival tradition despite heavy rain, sensing 'this is our family's way'.

passage:
On Gurpurab morning in their Ludhiana home, Tejas, five, tied a small orange patka on his head, with Mummy's help.

"Why do we go to the gurdwara so early?" he asked.

"Because in our family we help cook the langar," Amandeep said. "Your Nanaji did it, and I did it."

In the langar hall, Tejas carried a basket of rotis and placed one on each plate. He copied the grown-ups, folding his hands. "Our family does this every year," he told the boy next to him.

qa.q: What did Tejas carry in the langar hall?
qa.a: He carried a basket of rotis and placed one on each plate.

qa.q: How can you tell Tejas felt proud of the family tradition?
qa.a: He told the boy next to him that their family does this every year, showing he feels part of it.

qa.q: How did Amandeep help Tejas understand the tradition?
qa.a: Amandeep explained it as something the family has always done, naming Nanaji and Amandeep's own turn, so he could see his place in it.

qa.q: What is it like for the boy next to Tejas to hear about his family's custom?
qa.a: He may feel curious, or share his own family's ways in return.

grounding: Shows a young child joining a family festival custom and saying 'this is what our family does'.
